title: Deterministic Verification with a Single Automated Repair for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We present a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of inserting a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial generation call per intent; that identical candidate reused for both baseline and guarded episodes) we generated N_pairs = 250 natural-language intents with gpt-5-mini and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes using model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial-generation calls + 1 repair). Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); paired contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired-bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered sim‑to‑real (production-like) confirmatory contrast was not executed; the reported confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition executed here. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived; preregistration SHA-256 = 7a984dbf..., and the immutable master-prompt reference is provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 = 1872df1e...).

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly investigated as intent‑to‑configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), producing device CLI sequences from operator intents. Stochastic generation raises operational risks: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local‑policy violations, and vendor‑CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or nonfunctional device changes. Deterministic validators and bounded repair stages (generate–verify–repair, GVR) are a common architectural mitigation: only validator‑passed candidates are accepted or a limited automated repair is attempted [1],[2].

Despite prior evidence that validators reduce mechanically checkable errors, it remains unclear how much marginal benefit such guardrails provide when modern LLM outputs already conform to validator encodings for constrained tasks. A particular methodological source of confusion is experimental semantics: when the same initial model candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate), any observed difference can only arise through downstream deterministic validation and permitted repair, not from different first‑pass generations. We therefore preregistered and executed a paired experiment under explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics to quantify the marginal verifier‑detected improvement and its uncertainty for a constrained set of NetOps intents.

Our contributions are: (1) a sealed, preregistered paired evaluation with shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates the validator+single‑repair marginal effect on identical generated candidates; (2) artifact‑grounded numeric reconciliation showing model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair) and the exact contingency counts; and (3) a concise interpretation of operational meaning, limitations, and reproducibility artifacts for practitioners and researchers considering GVR guardrails in NetOps pipelines.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and empirical studies document LLM feasibility for drafting device configurations while repeatedly stressing the need for verification or human oversight [1],[2]. Deterministic network verification tools and header‑space/model‑checking approaches provide mechanized checks for forwarding, reachability, and many local‑policy properties and are commonly used as validators in GVR workflows [3],[4]. Generate‑and‑repair patterns and program‑repair methods have improved detection and correction of mechanically verifiable defects in code and configuration domains, but evaluations vary in scope and many studies remain emulation or bench oriented [5],[6]. Security analyses of prompt‑injection and retrieval threats emphasize filtering and validation layers but show adaptive adversaries are still an open concern for deployed pipelines [7].

This study differs by (a) enforcing shared_initial_candidate semantics so the paired comparison measures only downstream validator+repair effects on identical candidates, (b) reporting reconciled provider‑call accounting and stage mappings, and (c) archiving validator traces and analysis artifacts that permit exact numeric reproduction of the reported contingency counts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 as a confirmatory paired binary design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration fixed the single‑repair policy, exclusion rules, analysis tests (exact McNemar two‑sided and paired‑bootstrap percentile CIs), and the model‑call budget. Preregistration SHA‑256 = 7a984dbf7265c9a7.... The confirmatory partition executed here is the synthetic/emulation partition only; the preregistered sim‑to‑real contrast was not executed and therefore is not part of the reported confirmatory estimand.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and provider accounting (explicit). Under the registered shared_initial_candidate design exactly one initial model‑generation call was produced per intent; that identical generated candidate was used in both episodes (baseline: accept candidate; guarded: deterministic validation ± one repair). Provider accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251, which decomposes as 250 shared_initial_generation calls + 1 repair call. The experimental adapter records stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1} while its condition_counts labeling may appear as {"shared":250, "guarded":1}; the paper therefore explicitly maps adapter labels to pipeline stages: the adapter's "shared" label denotes the shared initial‑generation stage (one per pair) and the adapter's "guarded" label in the audit corresponds to the single repair‑stage call that occurred. This mapping is recorded in the deterministic reconciliation artifact (SHA‑256 = 91b0c6be...).

Task bank and constraints. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 250 constrained intents. Each task payload encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, all‑down‑before field change). Tasks were labeled medium/hard/very_hard and designed to exercise ordering and local workflow invariants without introducing open‑ended ambiguity. The full task manifest and representative payloads are archived in the evidence bundle.

Model invocation, guarded pipeline, and repairs. The declared model for initial generation was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). For each intent one shared initial generation call produced the candidate. The guarded pipeline submitted that candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic parsing, required_sequence checking, workflow constraints, and final_state snapshot comparison to the task's expected_final_state. If the validator returned valid = false for a guarded episode, the pipeline permitted up to one automated, template‑driven repair attempt limited to deterministic syntactic and ordering fixes (e.g., reorder commands to match required_sequence, split/join command lines). No multi‑iteration repairs or human escalation were permitted by design. Repair templates and validator encodings are recorded in the archived repair/validator traces.

Inclusion/exclusion and contamination handling. The preregistration excluded outputs that prevented deterministic verification (vendor‑parser failures), contained credential‑like tokens, or matched denylist hashes. Contamination detectors flagged instruction‑like embedded tokens; flagged items would be excluded from primary analysis and handled in sensitivity analyses. In this confirmatory run no episodes were excluded or flagged; complete_pair_count = 250 and the contamination summary is empty.

Analysis plan. The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1: an exact two‑sided McNemar test on paired binary outcomes plus a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the guarded − baseline difference (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary descriptive analyses (per‑difficulty, parsed_command diagnostics) were exploratory and reported with CIs only.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. Execution completed the preregistered confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, and complete_pair_count = 250. Provider accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 (completed), decomposing into stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}; model_calls_used = 251 reconciles to 250 shared initial generations plus a single repair call (deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 91b0c6be...). No provider calls failed and no cross‑condition cache reuse was recorded.

Primary binary outcomes and contingency. Deterministic validator results (full_intent_constraint_validation) produced baseline_success_count = 249/250 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996) and guarded_success_count = 250/250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table observed is n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The single discordant pair (baseline = fail, guarded = pass) corresponds to the only repair that was exercised; thus the repair‑conversion rate on the confirmatory partition is 1/250 = 0.4%.

Statistical inference. Exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the guarded − baseline paired difference (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (i.e., 0 – 1.2 percentage points). These outputs and the contingency CSV are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 087550a3..., analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 2de9aaf7...).

Representative validator diagnostics. Passed episodes show parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count derived from the task payload's required_sequence. Example: task‑000003 (hard) shows parsed_command_count = 6 and required_command_count = 6 with valid = true in both baseline and guarded episodes (scoring artifact SHA‑256 = 672c0dde...). Representative raw responses and normalized configurations are archived in the responses and scoring artifacts.

Repairs exercised. Exactly one automated repair call occurred and it converted the sole failing candidate into a validator pass; no other repairs were necessary or invoked across the confirmatory partition. Contamination detectors did not flag any confirmatory episodes, and no episodes were excluded per the preregistered rules.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting the near‑null marginal effect. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the constrained synthetic/emulation task bank, the marginal verifier‑detected benefit of inserting deterministic validation plus a single automated repair was small: initial gpt-5-mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing case via the single permitted repair. The paired‑bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) quantifies the maximum plausible verifier‑detected improvement under these task and pipeline constraints.

Factors explaining the small measured effect. Artifact‑grounded explanations are: (1) constrained task generation reduced linguistic and operational ambiguity, favoring well‑formed CLI outputs; (2) the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) produced syntactically well‑formed candidates for these constrained intents; and (3) the deterministic validator checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, expected_final_state snapshot) and does not capture broader dynamic or vendor‑semantic correctness beyond the encoded checks.

Statistical power and preregistered assumptions. The preregistration power calculation assumed baseline ≈ 0.90 to detect a 15 pp absolute effect with ≈80% power and thus selected N_pairs = 250. The realized baseline pass rate (0.996) substantially exceeded the prior assumption and thereby reduced power to detect small absolute improvements; accordingly, the paired‑bootstrap CI is the more informative operational bound than a null‑hypothesis significance outcome.

Scope limits and operational implications. Internal validity depends on prompt templates, the single‑repair policy, shared_initial_candidate semantics, and the validator encoding. Construct validity: the deterministic validator measures mechanically checkable correctness but not live protocol dynamics or emergent cross‑device behaviors. External validity is limited: the confirmatory evidence covers only the synthetic/emulation partition; production‑like and community partitions were not executed here. Security evaluations (adaptive prompt‑injection, retrieval attacks) and multi‑model comparisons remain unaddressed.

Practical takeaway. For tightly constrained emulation‑style tasks and a capable LLM, the marginal verifier‑detected improvement from inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair may be small. This should not be taken as a general recommendation to omit validators: (a) validators with broader encodings or additional dynamic tests could detect errors not exercised here; (b) multi‑iteration repairs, escalation, or richer testing chains could yield larger operational benefits; and (c) production heterogeneity and adversarial conditions may materially change the benefit calculus.
sections.conclusion: We ran a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics to quantify the verifier‑detected marginal effect of a deterministic validator plus one automated repair on identical LLM‑generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intents produced with gpt‑5‑mini, initial candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the guarded pipeline converted the single failing case via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). We emphasize the report’s limited confirmatory scope: the preregistered sim‑to‑real contrast was not executed, and the confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition. Broader production, adversarial, multi‑model, and multi‑iteration repair evaluations are necessary to establish generality. All execution and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper are archived and auditable from the preregistration and reconciliation artifacts cited in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer‑review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre‑lock infrastructure development; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and adapter: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider label: openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode as specified in the preregistration.

Preregistration and immutable prompt references: preregistration study id = study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 = 7a984dbf7265c9a7...). Immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Key reconciliation artifact: deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA‑256 = 91b0c6be4fb8...). The full execution and analysis manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and artifact hashes referenced in this manuscript are archived in the evidence bundle associated with the preregistration; the preregistration SHA above and the reconciliation SHA provide the archived manifest entry points for audit.

Executed confirmatory estimand and deviation disclosure: The preregistration included multiple partitions (synthetic/emulation, community, production‑like) and a preregistered sim‑to‑real contrast. Deviation disclosure (explicit): the preregistered sim‑to‑real/production‑like confirmatory comparison was not executed in this run; the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated on the synthetic/emulation partition only (N_pairs = 250; shared_initial_candidate semantics). Provider accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1} as recorded in the reconciliation artifact (SHA‑256 above).
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed.
Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, final_state snapshot) but did not measure dynamic protocol behavior or emergent cross‑device correctness.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi‑model or alternate‑validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi‑iteration repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval‑based attacks (adaptive prompt‑injection, vendor‑targeted exploit vectors) and large‑scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
